title: Lead Exposure During Paint Removal
summary: Blasting, sanding, scraping, or torch-cutting old paint can create lead dust and fumes that damage the lungs, brain, and liver and can follow you home on your clothes.
talking_points: Removing lead paint by blasting, sanding, scraping, or torch-cutting creates lead fumes and dust. Lead dust can settle on your clothes and hands and get into food and drink.
Lead can travel home on clothing, lunch pails, and shoes and harm the people you live with, especially children.
Never blast, sand, or cut with a torch any surface that might contain lead until it has been tested for lead.
If the surface has lead, your employer should give you a vacuum attachment for your equipment to capture the dust.
Using a chemical stripper: read the label and wear the PPE it calls for, such as coveralls, gloves, disposable shoe covers, vented goggles or a face shield with goggles, and a respirator.
Wash your hands and face before you eat, drink, or use tobacco. Never eat, drink, or use tobacco in the work area.
OSHA requires your employer to give you training, the right tools, and PPE. If you work around high lead levels, they must also test your blood.

In one story, a bridge worker removing lead paint for months ended up in the hospital with vomiting, weight loss, and trouble concentrating, and had high lead in his blood. Good practice: if you have symptoms like these, tell a doctor you work with lead and ask about a blood test.
site_hazards_to_check: Old painted surfaces that have not been tested for lead
Blasting, sanding, scraping, or torch work on painted surfaces
No vacuum attachment on sanders or grinders
Eating, drinking, or smoking in the work area
Lead dust on clothes, shoes, or lunch areas
discussion_questions: Has this surface been tested for lead, and where are the results?
What are we using to capture dust, and what PPE do we wear for this job?
How do we keep lead dust from going home with us?
